Normal-Form Games and Best Responses

Look directly at the two-player payoff table. Each of the four cells lists both players' payoffs. In each column, mark the first player's best answer. In each row, mark the second player's best answer. The cell where both marks land gets a star. That cell is a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium. Neither player wants to move away alone. For example, say you and a 🧑 friend each pick heads or tails on a coin. If your friend picks heads, one answer is best for you. Your pick likewise settles your friend's best answer. The pairing where both answers point at each other is the equilibrium.

Examples & Exercises

In the Prisoner's Dilemma, find every best response and show the pure-strategy Nash equilibrium is unique.

CDC(3,3)(0,5)D(5,0)(1,1)\begin{matrix} & C & D \\ C & (3,3) & (0,5) \\ D & (5,0) & (1,1) \end{matrix}CD​C(3,3)(5,0)​D(0,5)(1,1)​
Show proof
  1. For player 1: against CCC, DDD wins 5>35 > 35>3; against DDD, DDD wins 1>01 > 01>0. So DDD is player 1's strictly dominant strategy. Symmetrically, DDD strictly dominates for player 2.
  2. Player 1's best response in each column is always DDD (bottom row); player 2's best response in each row is always DDD (right column). The only cell where both hold is (D,D)(D, D)(D,D) — the unique pure-strategy Nash equilibrium. It is Pareto dominated by (C,C)(C, C)(C,C)'s (3,3)(3, 3)(3,3), but the unilateral incentive to deviate never disappears.

Find all pure-strategy Nash equilibria of the Stag Hunt game and compare their Pareto ranking.

SHS(4,4)(0,3)H(3,0)(3,3)\begin{matrix} & S & H \\ S & (4,4) & (0,3) \\ H & (3,0) & (3,3) \end{matrix}SH​S(4,4)(3,0)​H(0,3)(3,3)​
Show proof
  1. Player 1's best responses: SSS against the SSS column (4>34 > 34>3), HHH against the HHH column (3>03 > 03>0). Symmetrically for player 2: SSS against the SSS row, HHH against the HHH row.
  2. The cells where both best-respond are (S,S)(S, S)(S,S) and (H,H)(H, H)(H,H) — two pure-strategy Nash equilibria. (S,S)(S, S)(S,S) Pareto-dominates (H,H)(H, H)(H,H) ((4,4)(4,4)(4,4) vs (3,3)(3,3)(3,3)). Yet (H,H)(H, H)(H,H) is still an equilibrium: if the other hunts hare, hare is my best reply too. Which equilibrium materializes is a matter of beliefs — the seed of the equilibrium selection problem.
